snapshot.title: SSC Quant: Percentage & Applications
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ SSC Quant Hook: 1/4 more: 1/5 less. 1/x more: 1/(x+1) less. x+y+xy/100. Table is key. 1/6: 16.66%. 1/8: 12.5%.

quick_notes.title: Fraction-Percentage Table (Memorize!)
quick_notes.explanation: A fraction shows a part of a whole, like one out of two equal pieces. A percentage is a way to express that same part out of one hundred. For example, one-half, written as 1/2, is the same as 50 percent, or 50 out of 100. Other common fractions and their matching percentages are: one-third (1/3) is 33.33%, one-fourth (1/4) is 25%, one-fifth (1/5) is 20%, one-sixth (1/6) is 16.66%, one-seventh (1/7) is 14.28%, one-eighth (1/8) is 12.5%, one-ninth (1/9) is 11.11%, and one-eleventh (1/11) is 9.09%. Memorizing this table helps you quickly convert between fractions and percentages in problems.

quick_notes.title: Basic Formula
quick_notes.explanation: Percentage change is a way to measure how much something has increased or decreased compared to its starting amount. The change is the difference between the new value and the original value. To find the percentage change, you divide that change by the original value, then multiply the result by 100. For example, if a price goes from 50 to 60, the change is 10, and 10 divided by 50 is 0.2, times 100 gives 20 percent increase. If the change is negative, that means a decrease.

quick_notes.title: Successive Percentage
quick_notes.detail: Net change : x + y + (xy/100). If one is decrease, take negative value. (e.g., +20% and -20% net : 20 - 20 - 400/100 : -4%).
quick_notes.explanation: Successive percentage means applying two percentage changes one after another, like a price first increasing by 20% and then decreasing by 20%. To find the overall or net percentage change, use the formula x plus y plus (x times y divided by 100), where x and y are the percentage changes. quick_notes.title: Consumption & Price
quick_notes.detail: If Price increases by x%, and Expenditure is constant, Consumption must decrease. (e.g., Price +25% (1/4), Consumption -20% (1/5)).
quick_notes.explanation: Consumption and Price When the price of something you buy goes up, if you do not change the total amount of money you spend, which is called your expenditure, then you must buy less of it, which is called your consumption. For example, if the price increases by twenty-five percent, that means for every one hundred rupees you used to spend, you now have to pay one hundred twenty-five rupees for the same amount. To keep your total spending the same, you have to reduce how much you buy by twenty percent, which means for every one hundred units you used to buy, you now buy only eighty units.

quick_notes.title: Voting/Examination
quick_notes.detail: Total votes : Valid votes + Invalid votes. Passing marks : Scored marks + Needed marks.
quick_notes.explanation: TITLE: Voting/Examination In an election, the total number of votes cast is the sum of valid votes, which are ballots counted for a candidate, and invalid votes, which are rejected because they are spoiled or unclear. For example, if 100 votes are cast and 10 are invalid, then the valid votes are 90. In an exam, the passing marks are the minimum score you need to pass, and they equal the marks you actually scored plus the additional marks you still need to reach that minimum. So if the passing marks are 40 and you scored 30, you need 10 more marks to pass. Both concepts work the same way: the total is made of what counts plus what does not count or what is missing.

lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Universal Comparison'. Percentage is the most used tool in arithmetic. In SSC, the 'Fraction-to-Percentage' table is your best friend. From 'Population growth' to 'Successive changes'—these patterns repeat. Do you know how much a 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease changes the value? Let's master the percentages today.
